newsitem.title: LEBANON: SOLIDERE SEES STRONG INVESTOR INTEREST.
newsitem.headline: SOLIDERE SEES STRONG INVESTOR INTEREST.

text.p: Solidere is experiencing strong Arab investor interest in real estate in the Beirut city centre it is redeveloping and is working on a number of deals, chairman Nasser Chamaa was quoted on Wednesday as saying.
Profits were expected to rise to $70 million in 1997 from $58 million in 1996, he told the Beirut daily as-Safir in an interview.
"We have recently noticed big interest by Arab investors in real estate in the commercial city centre. We are working on a number of deals you will hear about soon," he said.
According to market sources Saudi Arabian billionaire Prince al-Waleed bin Talal is involved in negotiations for the construction of a Four Seasons hotel in the city centre.
Solidere's sales target for 1997 is $150 million and the company is confident that this can be met, a source said.
Chamaa told as-Safir that Solidere, which began rebuilding the war-damaged city centre in 1995, had so far signed contracts totalling $209 million for the sale of land to developers.
The price of land in the district had now risen to $1,050 per square metre from $950 when Solidere began selling plots, he said.
He indicated that the total cost of the construction and restoration of buildings to be carried out in the city centre by Solidere and private investors in the next few years would be $600 million.
Solidere had launched a programme to build or restore buildings totalling 300,000 square metres at a cost of $300 million and the rest would be carried out by private investors.
A market source told Reuters Solidere's building and restoration programme covered the period up to 1999.

It included construction of a 25,000 square metres U.N. building that has already begun, restoration of buildings covering 90-100,000 square metres, construction of souks (markets) totalling 100,000 square metres, of government buildings covering 70,000 square metres and of residential buildings totalling 30,000 square metres, the source said.

Chamaa said that in addition to the company's programme, developers who had bought land so far would spend an estimated $200 million to build on it, and pre-war property owners who had retained their buildings in the city centre would spend some $100 million on redeveloping them.
